Title: Question about rule on deck limit

Messages.Author: cantila
Messages.Body:
Why's there a rule that puts a cap on the maximum amount of cards you
can have in your library? I really don't see the point of this rule.
The more cards you have, the less chance you'll draw the cards you only
have one or two of, so it evens out the fact that you have a(very
small) advantage by not risking to run out of cards if you have say 130
cards in your deck. I also think that many times you can't include some
cards you'd like to, because of the deck limit. Cards that doesn't have
the highest priority but which you'd include more for fun (but would be
too "expensive" to include in a 90 slot deck) which makes more cards
wallpapered (if not completely than at least more than before). Also
combat decks have a disdvantage with the max cap rule since you
generaly brun cards much faster if you play a combat deck, so they're
likely to run out of cards sooner than others.

cantila <rogc...@student.luth.se> wrote:
> Why's there a rule that puts a cap on the maximum amount of cards you
> can have in your library? I really don't see the point of this rule.

V:TES is a game of resource management. I'd suspect that the player
who has the larger collection would benefit from unlimited deck size.
Since you replace a card once its played, an ultimate deck size is
needed to keep the playing field a bit more level between players.
This (along with the fact that many good V:TES strategies are rooted in
good, readily available common cards) is part of what keeps veteran
players with large collections from running away with the game. Also,
there is a certain appealing thematic air to having to rely on what
you've got in play when you've run out of cards. It's a testimony to a
player's deck building ability if they can gain VP after running out of
cards...

> The more cards you have, the less chance you'll draw the cards you
only
> have one or two of, so it evens out the fact that you have a(very
> small) advantage by not risking to run out of cards if you have say
130
> cards in your deck.

Again, this would only hold for those who didn't have ample cards
available.

>I also think that many times you can't include some
> cards you'd like to, because of the deck limit. Cards that doesn't
have
> the highest priority but which you'd include more for fun (but would
be
> too "expensive" to include in a 90 slot deck) which makes more cards
> wallpapered (if not completely than at least more than before). Also
> combat decks have a disdvantage with the max cap rule since you
> generaly brun cards much faster if you play a combat deck, so they're
> likely to run out of cards sooner than others.
>
>

Many groups use some means of limitation to deckbuilding in their
groups, so that esoteric ideas can be explored. The idea of unlimited
deck size could be one of those. Others simply rate decks in a manner
so that everyone knows what level of play intensity to expect. (eg.
some arbitrary scale like Tournament, Well-tuned, Rough, Experimental,
Goof-ball ;-) You may find that using a system like this will go
farther in allowing you to play those less used cards than an unlimited
deck size would. Using the above allowed me to build a Violet Tremain
Depravity plus Setite Corruption deck that had a chance to get off the
ground (but only in an Expeimental level game :-)

As for combat decks, yes, they do need to be very aware of how they
consume their resources. But how much worse would it be when thier
prey no longer have to worry aobut running out of S:CE (or maneuvers,
or whatever defense they choose)? Combat decks are more concerned with
getting the right mix of cards in their hand at a given time, than they
are with raw number of cards. That's why I'm so happy with Storage
Annex and WMO. Resources like that go much further in helping Combat
out, don't you think?

Regards,
R. David Zopf

Messages.Author: Halcyan 2
Messages.Body:
>Why's there a rule that puts a cap on the maximum amount of cards you
>can have in your library?

Several reasons.

First of all, library cards are a resource. Just like vampires and permanents,
library cards should be treated as a resource. One of the neatest things about
Jyhad is you often have to carefully consider whether to discard and then what
to discard (like that post on the best choice in a particular game). If you do
decide to discard (to get a card you want), you have to sacrifice a resource (1
card). If there was no limit to deck size, then they'd essentially be no
penalty for discarding. Cards like The Barrens and Fragment would be insanely
useful since cycling is then the key to winning.

Also, it would throw off some of the balance in meta-game. There are some decks
that rely on speed (i.e. some rush decks, etc.) -- using lots of cards to hit
hard. They might take out an opponent or two but then run out of steam (cards).
It is only the library card limit that prevents them from being able to easily
overwhelm the entire table.

Finally, one of favorite things about Jyhad is card balance. Unlike in Magic,
where usually one card is definitely better than another, just about all of the
Jyhad cards are balanced. Take Short Term Investment from Protracted Investment
(got it right this time! No more "Long Term" mistakes!). Protracted may seem
bad because it costs 3 pool and it takes 6 master phases to get all the pool
from it, but you can get 3 pool from one card. With Short Term, there's only a
net of 2 pool. With no card limit, there's no reason why you'd play with
Protracted (we're forgetting about Secret Horde right now BTW), but with a 90
card limit, you have to weigh your options carefully.

Halcyan 2

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
cantila wrote:
>
> Why's there a rule that puts a cap on the maximum amount of cards you

> can have in your library? I really don't see the point of this rule.

(Again, my original reply didn't make it far, so here it is again)

You'd have to ask the designer, Richard Garfield, that one. But here's
a reasonable guess:

Since VTES uses the draw-as-you-play rule, the deck size rule was
implemented to promote a player's desire to get more use out of
each card (and thus reduce the "benefit" of cycling cards for little
or no useful effect).

The replacement mechanism for the uncontrolled region (as opposed to
the hand) is not a convenient, and therefore could be used to explain
why there's not an upper limit on the size of your crypt.

> The more cards you have, the less chance you'll draw the cards you
> only have one or two of,

Which isn't a concern to some decks (having more than two copies of
every card). But even so, the cards you have only one copy of tend to
be the cards you don't rely on, so it's no drawback to reduce your
chance of drawing them.

> so it evens out the fact that you have a(very
> small) advantage by not risking to run out of cards if you have say

> 130 cards in your deck. I also think that many times you can't include

> some cards you'd like to, because of the deck limit. Cards that
> doesn't have the highest priority but which you'd include more for fun
> (but would be too "expensive" to include in a 90 slot deck) which
> makes more cards wallpapered (if not completely than at least more
> than before). Also combat decks have a disdvantage with the max cap
> rule since you generaly brun cards much faster if you play a combat
> deck, so they're likely to run out of cards sooner than others.

A deck that plays more cards per turn will run out of cards sooner,
emphasizing the need to make every card count.

And other ("slower") deck archetypes have disadvantages of their own.
